clue.text: Crayon representation of humorists

parts.note: Geoffrey Crayon was Washington Irving's pen name, and the book he published under it in 1822 carried the subtitle 'The Humorists'

explanation.surface: A coloured-pencil sketch of a group of comedians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crayon' looks like a drawing tool but is Washington Irving's pseudonym Geoffrey Crayon; his 1822 sketch book about an English country house is subtitled 'The Humorists'.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue names the pseudonymous author and the subtitle of Irving's book about a squire's English manor house.

clue.text: A handsome rise in France for English dramatist ()

parts.note: a beau is a handsome man, from the French word for handsome
mont is French for a mountain, a rise in the land

explanation.surface: A good-looking climb in France suits an English playwright.
explanation.walkthrough: Francis Beaumont was the Jacobean playwright who wrote in partnership with John Fletcher.
explanation.definitionFit: Francis Beaumont was an English playwright of the early seventeenth century, Fletcher's collaborator.

clue.text: Milton's monotheistic kind of mind-set

parts.note: describes the poet's theology, which rejected the doctrine of three persons in one God and held to one God alone

explanation.surface: A description of John Milton's religious outlook.
explanation.walkthrough: Milton's treatise De Doctrina Christiana denies that the Son is equal with the Father, a position against the doctrine of the Trinity.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who rejects the Christian doctrine of the Trinity holds to strict monotheism, as Milton did.

clue.text: Quote me about purgative

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the words for quote and me are read backwards as one run

parts.note: to quote a source is to cite it

explanation.surface: Someone asks to be quoted on the subject of laxatives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like 'concerning' but is the reversal signal, turning the whole run round; 'Quote me' sounds like a speaker inviting citation.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that causes vomiting purges the stomach, so it is a kind of purgative.

clue.text: Friend of Landor got up with my real problem

parts.note: rose is the past tense of rise, to get up

indicators.note: a problem is something to be worked out, so the letters of my real are to be worked into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone close to the poet Landor gets out of bed with a real difficulty of their own.
explanation.walkthrough: 'problem' signals the anagram of MY REAL, giving AYLMER. Walter Savage Landor wrote the elegy 'Rose Aylmer' for a young friend who died in India.
explanation.definitionFit: Rose Aylmer was a young woman Landor knew in Wales and mourned in his famous short elegy.

clue.text: The marchioness's swiveller

parts.note: in The Old Curiosity Shop the servant girl nicknamed the Marchioness marries the clerk Mr Swiveller, so this asks for his first name in its short form

explanation.surface: A noblewoman's rotating gadget.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swiveller' reads as something that swivels, but it is the surname of the clerk in The Old Curiosity Shop, whom the 'Marchioness' nurses and later marries.
explanation.definitionFit: The novel's clerk Richard Swiveller is always called by the short form of his first name.

clue.text: Quadroon. Stowed with Tom

parts.note: points to the young girl of mixed race in Uncle Tom's Cabin who is sold to Legree with Tom and shipped down the river with him

explanation.surface: Two terse notes on a slave cargo: a mixed-race girl, packed aboard alongside Tom.
explanation.walkthrough: In Harriet Beecher Stowe's novel the quadroon girl is bought by Simon Legree at the same auction as Uncle Tom and carried with him to his plantation.
explanation.definitionFit: Stowe's quadroon girl Emmeline shares Tom's fate, sold and shipped with him to Legree.

clue.text: Swallow writer's creation given new lease of life by Moore

definitions.text: Swallow writer's creation given new lease of life by Moore

parts.words: Swallow writer's creation given new lease of life by Moore
parts.note: Swallow is a novel by H. Rider Haggard; his best-known hero was revived by the comics writer Alan Moore

explanation.surface: A bird-writer's invention brought back to life by someone called Moore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swallow' looks like the bird or a gulp but is Haggard's 1899 novel; Alan Moore brought Haggard's big-game hunter back in The League of Extraordinary Gentlemen.
explanation.definitionFit: Haggard's hunter hero of King Solomon's Mines was later revived by Alan Moore in his comic series.

clue.text: Bulwer —— Strachey, literary men

parts.note: the gap is a name that ends one writer's name and begins another's: the novelist Edward Bulwer and the biographer Giles Strachey

explanation.surface: A fill-in-the-blank naming two writers.
explanation.walkthrough: One word completes both: the Victorian novelist Bulwer-Lytton and Lytton Strachey, author of Eminent Victorians.
explanation.definitionFit: The name is the second half of Bulwer-Lytton's surname and the first name of the biographer Strachey.

clue.text: A neat sort of American giant — an unbeatable wrestler in Libya

definitions.text: giant — an unbeatable wrestler in Libya

indicators.note: a sort of something is a version of it, so the letters of a neat are taken in a different arrangement

explanation.surface: A tidy kind of American strongman, unbeatable at wrestling in North Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' is the anagram signal on A NEAT. The Libyan giant drew his strength from his mother Earth until Heracles held him off the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth this son of Gaia was a giant of Libya who stayed undefeated in wrestling while touching the earth.

clue.text: Arrived with sale item at court

parts.note: came is a synonym of arrived
a lot is an item put up at an auction sale

explanation.surface: Someone turns up at a royal court with something bought at an auction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'court' is King Arthur's, a royal household, not a law court.
explanation.definitionFit: King Arthur's legendary castle stands for his whole royal household.

clue.text: Yale is so fabulous

definitions.meaning: a yale is a heraldic beast with swivelling horns, a creature of legend rather than nature
fabulous in its old sense means belonging to fable, invented

explanation.surface: Someone praises the American university as wonderful.
explanation.walkthrough: Yale reads as the university, but it is the heraldic beast; 'fabulous' means 'of fable', not 'splendid'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a heraldic yale and anything fabulous belong to legend and fable rather than fact.

clue.text: King of Naples is some sort of royal on solitary island

indicators.note: some of the letters of the following words are taken, a run lying across them

explanation.surface: The King of Naples is a kind of royal stranded on a lonely island.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface paints The Tempest, where the King of Naples is shipwrecked on Prospero's island; the name is spelt across 'royAL ON SOlitary'.
explanation.definitionFit: Alonso is the King of Naples in Shakespeare's The Tempest.

clue.text: The poet could be thus erotic

indicators.note: the letters of thus erotic could be arranged into a name, which signals an anagram

explanation.surface: A poet who might be this sensual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be' rearranges THUS EROTIC; the Greek poet of Sicily invented pastoral verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Theocritus was the Greek pastoral poet of the third century BC.

clue.text: Bleak sort of film featuring Niro perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the letters of the actor's surname may be ordered some other way

explanation.surface: A dark kind of movie starring Robert De Niro, maybe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges NIRO; De Niro's crime films make the surface plausible.
explanation.definitionFit: Film noir is the dark, pessimistic genre of crime movies, from the French for black.

clue.text: Greene's eponymous ruler

parts.note: Robert Greene, the Elizabethan playwright, named a play after a king of Aragon

explanation.surface: A monarch who gives his name to a work by Greene.
explanation.walkthrough: Not Graham Greene: Robert Greene's play is The Comical History of Alphonsus, King of Aragon (about 1587).
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Greene's play takes its title from its hero, a King of Aragon.

clue.text: Gothic stepdame in unseemly rush

indicators.note: the Goths were barbarians who wrecked what they found, so Gothic signals the letters of stepdame are knocked about

explanation.surface: A wicked stepmother in a Gothic novel runs about in an unladylike hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gothic' suggests a horror-novel stepmother, but it signals the anagram of STEPDAME.
explanation.definitionFit: A stampede is a sudden headlong rush, of a herd or a crowd, without any dignity.

clue.text: Dell revealing unreliable chap

definitions.meaning: Ethel M. Dell, the popular romantic novelist, published a book with this title in 1914
a cheat who cannot be trusted with money

explanation.surface: A wooded valley shows up an untrustworthy man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dell' looks like a small valley, but it is the novelist Ethel M. Dell, whose title names a cheat.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethel M. Dell's novel bears the name, and a fraudster is a man not to be trusted.

clue.text: Albert's man, his fate creating Christmas work for China

definitions.text: Albert's man, his fate creating Christmas work for China

parts.words: Albert's man, his fate creating Christmas work for China
parts.note: Susan Wittig Albert's mystery is named after a man whose death gives her sleuth China Bayles a case at Christmas; the first word of its title is wanted

explanation.surface: Prince Albert's servant meets a fate that makes festive work for the Chinese.
explanation.walkthrough: Albert is the crime writer Susan Wittig Albert and China her herbalist detective China Bayles; her novel Mistletoe Man turns on the death of the man who supplies the plant.
explanation.definitionFit: The plant hung at Christmas gives the first word of Albert's title, Mistletoe Man, a seasonal case for China Bayles.

clue.text: "Among the most noisome of the s and dens of London" (Oliver Twist)

definitions.text: "Among the most noisome of the s and dens of London" (Oliver Twist)

parts.words: "Among the most noisome of the s and dens of London" (Oliver Twist)
parts.note: a quotation from Dickens with a word removed from the gap before the s; the missing word is an old term for a brothel or low haunt

explanation.surface: A line from Dickens about the filthiest corners of London.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap is filled by the missing word, with the printed s making its plural: stews were brothels or squalid dens.
explanation.definitionFit: In old English usage a stew is a brothel or squalid den, which fits the quotation's gap.

clue.text: Blue engine assembled by clergyman

parts.note: the Reverend W. Awdry created the Railway Series of talking engines, and one of the early ones is painted blue

explanation.surface: A sad motor put together by a vicar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue' reads as sad, and 'assembled' suggests building, but the clergyman is the Rev. W. Awdry, whose Railway Series includes a blue engine of this name.
explanation.definitionFit: In Awdry's Railway Series this blue tank engine is one of Thomas's oldest friends.

clue.text: May be honest as a gorgon

indicators.note: the letters of honest may be arranged into another word, which marks an anagram

explanation.surface: Even a monster may be truthful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'May be' rearranges HONEST; she is one of Medusa's two immortal sisters.
explanation.definitionFit: Stheno is one of the three Gorgon sisters of Greek myth, alongside Euryale and Medusa.

clue.text: US legal man, inwardly hurt, demonstrates Buddhist law

indicators.note: inwardly says the word for hurt goes inside the letters for the American lawyer

parts.note: DA, District Attorney, is an American public prosecutor
harm is a synonym of hurt

explanation.surface: An American prosecutor, wounded inside, sets out Buddhist teaching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inwardly hurt' sounds like grief, but 'inwardly' is the container signal; DA, District Attorney, is the American prosecutor.
explanation.definitionFit: In Buddhism dharma is the cosmic law and the teaching of the Buddha.

clue.text: Finished author's siblings

parts.note: haggard means worn out or finished, so the finished author is H. Rider Haggard, who wrote a novel about brothers

explanation.surface: The brothers and sisters of a writer who has completed a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finished' stands for 'haggard', worn out, giving H. Rider Haggard, whose 1904 crusader novel The Brethren follows two brothers.
explanation.definitionFit: Haggard's novel title is an old plural meaning brothers, the siblings of the clue.

clue.text: Sea goddess in some twice-told tale

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held 'Sea goddess in some twice-told tale (4)': LETO is not spelt in 'twice-told tale' forwards or backwards (only in a reordered 'tale told'), and Leto is no sea goddess; the clue looks garbled in OCR and no source gives the printed text.
annotationWithheld.clue: Sea goddess in some twice-told tale

clue.text: Possibly be a line to scene of Western showdown

indicators.note: possibly hints that the letters of be a line could form another word, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Perhaps a single line leads to the setting of a cowboy gunfight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' rearranges BE A LINE into the Kansas cattle town of the Wild West.
explanation.definitionFit: Abilene in Kansas was a wild cattle-trail town and the setting of many Western gunfights.

clue.text: Autumnal reflections by Camus in translation?

definitions.text: Autumnal reflections by Camus in translation?

parts.words: Autumnal reflections by Camus in translation?
parts.note: Camus's novel La Chute has an English title that is also the American word for autumn

explanation.surface: Seasonal musings by Albert Camus, rendered into English.
explanation.walkthrough: Camus's La Chute is a monologue of self-reflection; its English title is also the American name for the autumn season.
explanation.definitionFit: The English title of La Chute doubles as the American word for the season of falling leaves.

clue.text: Where English journeyman, say, dramatizes a bit of a nasty turn?

definitions.text: Where English journeyman, say, dramatizes a bit of a nasty turn?

parts.words: Where English journeyman, say, dramatizes a bit of a nasty turn?
parts.note: J. B. Priestley wrote the travel book English Journey, so he is the English journeyman, and his 1932 play is named after a risky bend in the road

explanation.surface: A traveller in England stages a scene on a treacherous bend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'English journeyman' is J. B. Priestley, author of English Journey; his first play takes its title from a hazardous bend.
explanation.definitionFit: Priestley's 1932 play takes its name from a risky bend, the kind of nasty turn the clue describes.
